title: Who spent your AI budget? LiteLLM tracks and caps it
description:
LiteLLM is an open-source AI gateway and Python SDK (open core) for calling 100+ LLM providers, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini and Bedrock, in one OpenAI-compatible format, with a virtual key per team, budgets, rate limits, spend tracking and fallbacks.
It's a self-hosted LLM gateway with an MIT-licensed core; SSO beyond 5 users, audit logs and other enterprise features need a paid licence.

In this video:
- What LiteLLM is and how the gateway works (one endpoint in the OpenAI format; it checks the key, routes the call and logs the cost)
- 3 real uses: switch models without rewriting code, give each team its own key and budget, stay up when a provider fails
- The catch: the open-core licence, the Postgres (and Redis) it needs, and its weekly release pace
- Who it's for, an alternative, and how to try it

Three real uses:
1. Switch models without rewriting code: the same completion() call in Python, or the OpenAI SDK pointed at the gateway, reaches OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Bedrock, Azure and the rest of its 100+ providers. You change the model name.
2. A key per team: virtual keys with their own allowed models, max_budget, budget_duration and rpm/tpm rate limits. Spend is logged per request, key, team and user. Once a key passes its budget, its requests fail.
3. Stay up when a provider fails: retries, load balancing across deployments, and fallbacks to another model, set in config.yaml (num_retries, fallbacks).

The catch: LiteLLM is open core. Code outside the enterprise/ folder is MIT; the enterprise/ folder is under a commercial licence that needs a paid subscription for production use, and the enterprise features are unlocked by a licence key in the same image. Paid features include SSO and SCIM (SSO is free for up to 5 users), audit logs, secret managers, per-team logging, spend reports, guardrails per key or team, and key rotation. Virtual keys, budgets and spend tracking need a Postgres database: without one, virtual keys don't work and budgets aren't enforced. Once you run more than one copy of the gateway, the docs say to add Redis 7.0 or newer so rate limits are shared. It moves fast: a new minor version every week (six since mid-September, up to 1.106.0), so pin the version you run, as the docs recommend. Keep the master key and salt key safe: the master key gives full admin access, and changing the salt key makes stored provider keys unreadable.

Try it (the Docker quick start in the docs):
curl -sSLO https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/raw/main/docker/docker-compose.quickstart.yml
Create a .env file with a LITELLM_MASTER_KEY and a LITELLM_SALT_KEY, as the quick start shows, then run:
docker compose -f docker-compose.quickstart.yml up -d
It starts the gateway on port 4000 and a Postgres database. Open http://localhost:4000/ui and sign in as admin with your master key. You need your own provider API key.
Python SDK only (Python 3.10 to 3.14): uv add litellm
